Frances Havergal
FRAN-sis HAV-ur-guhl
proper noun (person)
English hymn writer (1836-1879), known as the "consecration poet," author of Take My Life and Let It Be.

📖 Biblical Definition

Frances Ridley Havergal was an English hymn writer and devotional poet, often called the "consecration poet" for the theme that runs through her best-loved hymns: the glad and total surrender of the whole life to Christ. A woman of deep personal piety, exceptional memory of Scripture, and frail health, she wrote hymns that have called generations of believers to wholehearted devotion. Chief among them is Take My Life, and Let It Be Consecrated, Lord, to Thee, which offers to God in turn the believer's hands, feet, voice, lips, silver and gold, will, heart, and self — a hymn she wrote after a night of rejoicing over the conversion of others, and whose own words she took with such seriousness that she later sent away her jewelry to be sold for missions. She also wrote Like a River Glorious, on the perfect peace of trusting God, and Who Is on the Lord's Side? Havergal stands in the dictionary as the poet of consecration, who taught the church that the only reasonable response to redeeming grace is the offering of the whole life to God, holding back nothing from the Savior who gave Himself wholly for us.

FRANCES HAVERGAL, proper noun. English hymn writer and devotional poet (1836-1879).

Known as the "consecration poet."

Author of Take My Life, and Let It Be Consecrated, Lord, to Thee.

Author of Like a River Glorious and Who Is on the Lord's Side?

Lived her hymns, even sending her jewelry to be sold for missions.

📖 Key Scripture

Rom 12:1 — "I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service."

Gal 2:20 — "I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me."

Isa 26:3 — "Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee."

2 Cor 5:15 — "And that he died for all, that they which live should not henceforth live unto themselves, but unto him which died for them, and rose again."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Havergal's hymns honor the recovery of wholehearted consecration to Christ, against a half-hearted religion that would receive His grace while withholding the life He bought.

expand to see more

Half-hearted-devotion correction. It is the perennial temptation to accept the gift of salvation while reserving large portions of life from the Giver. Havergal's Take My Life refuses the reservation, offering to God hands, voice, will, heart, and self, holding nothing back. The dictionary holds that the mercies of God call for the presenting of the whole body as a living sacrifice (Rom 12:1); grace received demands a life surrendered, and to keep back parts of ourselves from Christ is to forget the price He paid.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the redeemed no longer live unto themselves. Christ died that those who live should live unto Him who died and rose for them (2 Cor 5:15). Havergal not only sang consecration but lived it, parting with her treasures for the gospel's sake. The dictionary commends her example: true faith works itself out in a life laid wholly on the altar, glad to belong entirely to the Savior who gave Himself entirely for us.
